title: Lecture 5 — Instructor Tutorial
subject: Algorithm Analysis
description: 12 questions transcribed from the instructor’s Tutorial 5: Randomized algorithms, randomized quicksort, and quickselect. Source questions, choices, and answer-key selections are preserved.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what is the primary reason for using randomness in algorithms?
options: To ensure the algorithm always finishes in the same amount of time.
To break ties and symmetry that could lead to predictable, worst-case behavior.
To eliminate the need for recursive functions in divide-and-conquer paradigms.
To guarantee that the algorithm is 100% accurate in all cases, unlike deterministic ones.
questions.correctAnswer: To break ties and symmetry that could lead to predictable, worst-case behavior.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: To break ties and symmetry that could lead to predictable, worst-case behavior.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a "Las Vegas" algorithm?
options: It always produces the correct answer, but its running time is a random variable.
It has a fixed, bounded running time but may produce an incorrect answer with a small probability.
It is designed specifically for gambling applications and probability simulations.
It is an approximation algorithm that yields "good enough" answers in linear time.
questions.correctAnswer: It always produces the correct answer, but its running time is a random variable.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects A: It always produces the correct answer, but its running time is a random variable.

questions.question: If an algorithm always runs in O(n log n) time but has a 1% probability of providing the wrong result, it is classified as:
options: A deterministic algorithm.
A Las Vegas algorithm.
A Monte Carlo algorithm.
An adversarial algorithm.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: A Monte Carlo algorithm.

questions.question: In deterministic Quicksort, which input type typically triggers the worst-case O(n²) runtime when the first element is consistently chosen as the pivot?
options: Randomized arrays.
Arrays with many duplicate values.
Already sorted or reverse-sorted arrays.
Very small arrays where n < 10.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: Already sorted or reverse-sorted arrays.

questions.question: How does the Randomized Quicksort algorithm modify the standard partitioning process?
options: It partitions the array into three parts instead of two.
It selects a random index i, swaps A[i] with the pivot position, and then partitions.
It sorts the array before selecting the median as a pivot.
It eliminates the recursion step to save space.
questions.correctAnswer: It selects a random index i, swaps A[i] with the pivot position, and then partitions.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: It selects a random index i, swaps A[i] with the pivot position, and then partitions.

questions.question: What is the expected number of comparisons E[C(n)] for Randomized Quicksort?
options: Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(log n)
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: Θ(n log n)

questions.question: Even with a random pivot strategy, what is the theoretical worst-case time complexity of Randomized Quicksort?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(2ⁿ)
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: O(n²)

questions.question: What is the main goal of the Quickselect algorithm?
options: To sort an entire array in linear time.
To find the k-th smallest element in an unsorted array.
To determine the maximum value in a balanced BST.
To select a random sample of data for statistical analysis.
questions.correctAnswer: To find the k-th smallest element in an unsorted array.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: To find the k-th smallest element in an unsorted array.

questions.question: Why is the expected runtime of Quickselect O(n), while Quicksort is O(n log n)?
options: Quickselect uses a faster partitioning method.
Quickselect only recurses into one side of the partition that contains the target element.
Quickselect does not use random pivots.
Quickselect requires the input array to be pre-sorted.
questions.correctAnswer: Quickselect only recurses into one side of the partition that contains the target element.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: Quickselect only recurses into one side of the partition that contains the target element.

questions.question: Which of the following is identified as a "common mistake" when implementing Quickselect?
options: Using recursion instead of iteration.
Picking the median of the array as the pivot.
Converting the global index k to a "rank within a subarray" without precise adjustment.
Using O(n) space for the partitioning step.
questions.correctAnswer: Converting the global index k to a "rank within a subarray" without precise adjustment.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: Converting the global index k to a "rank within a subarray" without precise adjustment.

questions.question: Which pivot strategy is described as "often better in practice" but still "not adversarially robust"?
options: First element.
Last element.
Median-of-three.
Random element.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects C: Median-of-three.

questions.question: Based on the lecture "Key Takeaways," randomized approaches are often preferred in practice because:
options: They are more complex and therefore more secure.
They have better expected performance and are robust against adversarial inputs.
They guarantee a O(log n) worst-case runtime for all sorting problems.
They eliminate the need for space complexity analysis.
questions.correctAnswer: They have better expected performance and are robust against adversarial inputs.
questions.explanation: The tutorial answer key selects B: They have better expected performance and are robust against adversarial inputs.
